items.note: Garbhādhāna rite: a casket holding the Seed and Germ of the temple is immured in the wall before construction.
Proportions of the garbha casket relative to the temple: width one twelfth of wall height, height half its width.
Grades of casket; the copper square casket of 8 finger widths seems generally in use.
Contents of the casket: Vāstumaṇḍala divinities and the wealth of the earth.
Lowering of the Garbha vessel to the foundation, with Ananta and the Earth maṇḍala drawn; casket as goddess Earth.
Mayamata: perfect measurement of the temple brings perfection in the universe.
Isānaśivagurudevapaddhati: the temple is made up of the presence of Śiva and Śakti; the concrete form of Śiva is the House of God.
Vimāna as a generally accepted name for temple; measure is identity with the object.
Temple defined as the main shrine with garbhagṛha; mandapa and other buildings are accessory and conform to the Vimāna's proportions.
Vimāna is built by proportionate measurement; module from the architecture or from the Liṅga or image.
Standard proportions: module is the width of the Prāsāda wall; garbhagṛha half the external width; height double the width.
Vimāna and Prāsāda are synonymous and the two most significant words for temple.
Amarakoṣa: Prāsādas are the residences of gods and kings.
In the Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra Prāśāda retains the sense of palace in one place, while in its temple chapters it most frequently designates the temple.
Earliest inscriptions using Prāśāda for a temple include a Garuḍa pillar from Bhilsa naming an uttama Prāśada of Bhagavat, 2nd century B.C.
refs: J. N. Banerjea, The Development of Hindu Iconography, p. 102

items.note: Meaning of Prasāda per the Iśānaśivagurudevapaddhati: temple made up of the presence of Śiva and Śakti and the Principles of Existence.
Five-faced, ten-handed Śiva image corresponding to the Prāsāda mantra, with the weapons and attributes listed.
The finial above the temple superstructure is the visual equivalent of Bindu.
The Prāsāda as symbolic substance corresponding to Nāda; the rhythmical plan shows the world is made from it.

items.note: Brhat Saṃhitā: building a temple as pious act; pūrta includes tanks, wells, lakes and houses of the gods.
Ancient extant temples and preserved texts date from about the same age; Bṛhat Saṃhitā and Matsya Purāṇa refer to earlier standard works.
Eighteen chief preceptors of Vāstuśāstra listed in the Matsyapurāṇa suggest many schools of architecture before the sixth century.
Prāsāda is the shell of the garbhagṛha, a small dark square chamber unchangeable throughout the ages.
Funds and decision to build came from the Yajamāna or Kāraka, who entrusted the work to priest and craftsman.
Darśana and pūjā are the purpose of visiting the temple; the temple is a tīrtha made by art.
Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra LVI on patron and architect of the Meru prāsāda.
Guilds of architects and potters levied a cess for temple maintenance (Kaman inscription c. 8th century).
Three vertical parts of the Prāsāda (socle, garbhagṛha, superstructure); a temple may have halls, subsidiary shrines, walls and gate towers.
Socle mouldings and vedikā embody memory of the altar; carved bands of men, horses and Kirttimukha, including in earlier Central Indian temples.
Vedi name is repeated on the upper śikhara, with āmalaka and finial above; the Vedic altar survives in lowest and highest parts.
Stone śikhara built by corbelling and covered by a horizontal plate; raised platforms below sixth century temples at Bhitargaon, Deogarh, Nachna Kuthara.
